We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Debiasing NLU Models via Causal Intervention and Counterfactual Reasoning
papers.research_question: How to reduce biases in NLU models that arise from spurious correlations in training data using causal inference?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a debiasing framework for NLU models using causal intervention and counterfactual reasoning to remove spurious correlations and hypothesis-only bias.
papers.conclusion: The proposed causal inference-based debiasing strategy is effective and agnostic to the base encoder models.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed CICR framework outperforms previous debiasing methods on bias-sensitive datasets (SNLI-hard and FEVER symmetric test sets) by large margins.
The method maintains the original in-distribution performance on SNLI and FEVER datasets.
Ablation studies show that both causal intervention and counterfactual reasoning components are effective.
future_direction: Developing a more complex causal graph with external knowledge within the counterfactual inference framework.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that strong Natural Language Understanding (NLU) models are prone to relying on annotation biases of the datasets as a shortcut, which goes against the underlying mechanisms of the task of interest. To reduce such biases, several recent works introduce debiasing methods to regularize the training process of targeted NLU models. In this paper, we provide a new perspective with causal inference to find out the bias. On one hand, we show that there is an unobserved confounder for the natural language utterances and their respective classes, leading to spurious correlations from training data. To remove such confounder, the backdoor adjustment with causal intervention is utilized to find the true causal effect, which makes the training process fundamentally different from the traditional likelihood estimation. On the other hand, in inference process, we formulate the bias as the direct causal effect and remove it by pursuing the indirect causal effect with counterfactual reasoning. We conduct experiments on large-scale natural language inference and fact verification benchmarks, evaluating on bias sensitive datasets that are specifically designed to assess the robustness of models against known biases in the training data. Experimental results show that our proposed debiasing framework outperforms previous state-of-the-art debiasing methods while maintaining the original in-distribution performance.

papers.title: Reasoning about Entailment with Neural Attention
papers.research_question: Can an end-to-end differentiable neural network with a word-by-word attention mechanism outperform existing methods for recognizing textual entailment (RTE)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural model based on LSTMs with a word-by-word attention mechanism for recognizing textual entailment, which outperforms previous neural and feature-based models, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the SNLI dataset.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that end-to-end differentiable neural models with attention can achieve state-of-the-art performance on textual entailment, and these general sequence models are suitable for transfer learning and application to other entailment tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Conditional encoding (processing the hypothesis conditioned on the premise) improves performance over encoding sentences independently.
Incorporating an attention mechanism provides further performance gains by allowing the model to focus on relevant parts of the premise.
Word-by-word attention yields the best performance, enabling fine-grained reasoning over entailments of individual words and phrases.
Two-way attention (attending in both directions) does not improve performance, likely due to the asymmetric nature of entailment.
Qualitative analysis of attention weights shows the model learns to attend to semantically relevant words and phrases, including synonyms and multi-word expressions.
papers.limitation:
Interpretations based on attention weights must be taken with care because the model is not forced to rely solely on the attention-weighted representation.
For longer premises, attention becomes more uniformly distributed, suggesting limitations when multiple words need to be considered.
future_direction: Focus on transfer learning tasks by pre-training the recurrent systems on other corpora and applying the models to other entailment tasks.
Scale the methods to larger units of text (e.g., paragraphs and entire documents) using hierarchical attention mechanisms.
Explore more structured forms of attention or other forms of differentiable memory to improve performance on RTE.
papers.abstract: While most approaches to automatically recognizing entailment relations have used classifiers employing hand engineered features derived from complex natural language processing pipelines, in practice their performance has been only slightly better than bag-of-word pair classifiers using only lexical similarity. The only attempt so far to build an end-to-end differentiable neural network for entailment failed to outperform such a simple similarity classifier. In this paper, we propose a neural model that reads two sentences to determine entailment using long short-term memory units. We extend this model with a word-by-word neural attention mechanism that encourages reasoning over entailments of pairs of words and phrases. Furthermore, we present a qualitative analysis of attention weights produced by this model, demonstrating such reasoning capabilities. On a large entailment dataset this model outperforms the previous best neural model and a classifier with engineered features by a substantial margin. It is the first generic end-to-end differentiable system that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on a textual entailment dataset.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: Causal Head Gating: A Framework for Interpreting Roles of Attention Heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models in a causal manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for causal interpretation of attention heads, and shows that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, head roles are low modularity, and instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: CHG is a flexible and scalable method for identifying causally relevant attention heads, revealing the distributed and context-dependent nature of computation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CHG scores yield causal insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analysis.
LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits.
Individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity).
Instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
CHG does not reveal the precise computations performed by individual heads.
Occasional divergence between G+ and G- scores.
Head roles are context-dependent and vary across runs.
future_direction: Build on these tools to develop circuit-level explanations of how models implement complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: We present causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for interpreting the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models. CHG learns soft gates over heads and assigns them a causal taxonomy - facilitating, interfering, or irrelevant - based on their impact on task performance. Unlike prior approaches in mechanistic interpretability, which are hypothesis-driven and require prompt templates or target labels, CHG applies directly to any dataset using standard next-token prediction. We evaluate CHG across multiple large language models (LLMs) in the Llama 3 model family and diverse tasks, including syntax, commonsense, and mathematical reasoning, and show that CHG scores yield causal, not merely correlational, insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analyses. We also introduce contrastive CHG, a variant that isolates sub-circuits for specific task components. Our findings reveal that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, that individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity), and that instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How do different mechanisms interact in the decision-making of LLMs? The paper proposes to trace how one mechanism becomes dominant in the final prediction.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formulates the competition of mechanisms and traces how mechanisms compete within LLMs, identifying critical components and attention positions that control the strength of mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates how to trace the competition of mechanisms in LLMs and reveals insights into how factual and counterfactual mechanisms interact and can be controlled.
papers.key_findings:
In early layers, the factual attribute is encoded in the subject position, while the counterfactual is in the attribute position.
The attention blocks write most of the factual and counterfactual information to the last position.
All the highly activated heads attend to the attribute position regardless of the specific type of information they promote. The factual information flows by penalizing the counterfactual attribute rather than promoting the factual one.
We can up-weight the value of a few very localized values of the attention head matrix to strengthen factual mechanisms substantially.
Similar tokens confuse the model more easily, and larger models suffer more from such confusion.
papers.limitation: Logit inspection can occasionally fail to reflect the actual importance of vocabulary items, especially in the early layers of the network.
future_direction: Extend the competition of mechanisms formulation to more complex mechanisms and multi-step reasoning.
Explore other mechanisms and their competitions in future work.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research aims to bridge the gap between empirical success and our scientific understanding of the inner workings of large language models (LLMs). However, most existing research focuses on analyzing a single mechanism, such as how models copy or recall factual knowledge. In this work, we propose a formulation of competition of mechanisms, which focuses on the interplay of multiple mechanisms instead of individual mechanisms and traces how one of them becomes dominant in the final prediction. We uncover how and where mechanisms compete within LLMs using two interpretability methods: logit inspection and attention modification. Our findings show traces of the mechanisms and their competition across various model components and reveal attention positions that effectively control the strength of certain mechanisms. Code: https://github.com/francescortu/comp-mech. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/francescortu/comp-mech.

papers.title: Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause\n Representations on Agreement Prediction
papers.research_question: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlterRep, a counterfactual intervention method to test if language models use linguistic features consistently with grammar, and finds that BERT uses relative clause boundary information grammatically and abstractly.
papers.conclusion: AlterRep provides a way to test causal use of linguistic features in models, and shows BERT uses relative clause boundaries grammatically and abstractly.
papers.key_findings:
Only middle layers of BERT causally influence agreement prediction in a manner consistent with English grammar, while all layers encode RC boundary information.
RC boundary representations partially generalize across different RC types, suggesting abstract representation.
Interventions using random subspaces do not yield interpretable changes, indicating specificity of RC subspaces.
Similar patterns observed in BERT variants of different sizes, except BERT-tiny.
papers.limitation: AlterRep uses linear subspaces to analyze non-linear networks, so negative results may not be conclusive.
future_direction: Apply AlterRep to test hypotheses about a wide range of linguistic structures and tasks.
papers.abstract:
When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use
their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar
of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address
this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep
generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is
encoded, while leaving intact all other aspects of the original representation.
By measuring the change in a model's word prediction behavior when these
counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can
draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question
on the model's behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of
different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use
RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent
with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to
a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT
represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.

papers.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the faithfulness of natural language explanations that claim individual neurons in a language model represent a concept?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework with observational and intervention modes to evaluate natural language explanations of neurons, and applies it to show that GPT-4-generated explanations for GPT-2 XL neurons have low faithfulness and causal efficacy.
papers.conclusion: Natural language may not be the best medium for model explanations due to vagueness and ambiguity, and neurons may not be the optimal unit of analysis; structured formalisms and analysis of neuron groups are promising alternatives.
papers.key_findings:
Even among the top 0.6% of neurons with GPT-4 explanation scores ≥0.8, explanations achieve only 0.64 precision and 0.50 recall.
Intervention-based evaluation shows GPT-4 explanations have little to no causal efficacy, performing similarly to random baselines.
Individual neurons are not effective causal mediators; causal effects require aggregating over many neurons, especially in early MLP layers.
Natural language explanations are often vague and ambiguous, making them unreliable for technical decision-making.
The GPT-4 score used by Bills et al. (2023) is insensitive to Type I errors and does not guarantee faithful explanations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on GPT-2 XL; results may not extend directly to other architectures.
Faithful explanations could be used for malicious manipulations of models.
future_direction: Use structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages) instead of natural language for explanations.
Analyze groups of neurons or other network components (e.g., attention heads, residual streams) as units of analysis.
Conduct similar evaluations on other model architectures.
papers.abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: A Modular Dataset to Demonstrate LLM Abstraction Capability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs have an internal representation of reasoning correctness and abstraction in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can a subtractive pruning-based probe (subnetwork probing) more faithfully detect linguistic properties encoded in a pre-trained model compared to traditional MLP probes, by being better at finding existing properties and worse at learning tasks on its own?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces subnetwork probing, a pruning-based method that finds a subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task, demonstrating it is more faithful to the model (higher accuracy on pre-trained, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominates MLP probes in accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful probing method than existing approaches for understanding what linguistic properties are encoded in pre-trained models, and it enables additional analysis through the subnetworks it discovers.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on the pre-trained model and lower accuracy on randomly initialized models compared to an MLP probe, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less capable of learning the task independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are localized in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks discovered by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: Illustrating a neural model of logic computations: The case of Sherlock Holmes' old maxim
papers.research_question: What is the cognitive reason for the feeling that Holmes' maxim is an evident truth? The paper postulates that it is because our brains have neural modules that perform modal logical computations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neural model based on matrix associative memories that can perform modal logical computations, explaining why humans accept Sherlock Holmes' maxim as true.
papers.conclusion: Our brains are equipped with neural modules capable of modal logical computations, which explains why we accept Holmes' maxim as true.
papers.key_findings:
The paper provides a neural model based on matrix associative memories that can perform logical operations.
It shows how modal logic operators (possibility and necessity) can be implemented in the model.
It demonstrates how Holmes' maxim can be represented and computed by the model.
It connects the model with subjective probabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical approach helps explain cognitive acceptability, but mathematics itself remains unexplained, making the explanation incomplete and provisional.
The link between cognitive probabilities and formal probabilities is left as an open problem.
future_direction: Exploring whether the process represents a class of nonmonotonic reasoning.
Investigating the link between cognitive probabilities and formal probabilities.
papers.abstract: Natural languages can express some logical propositions that humans are able to understand. We illustrate this fact with a famous text that Conan Doyle attributed to Holmes: 'It is an old maxim of mine that when you have excluded the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth'. This is a subtle logical statement usually felt as an evident truth. The problem we are trying to solve is the cognitive reason for such a feeling. We postulate here that we accept Holmes' maxim as true because our adult brains are equipped with neural modules that naturally perform modal logical computations.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Can Subnetwork Structure be the Key to Out-of-Distribution Generalization?
papers.research_question: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? The paper investigates whether subnetworks within biased models can achieve better OOD performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that biased models contain unbiased functional subnetworks, proposes the functional lottery ticket hypothesis, and introduces Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) to improve OOD generalization by learning subnetwork structures.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork structure is a key factor for out-of-distribution generalization, and the proposed Modular Risk Minimization method effectively learns such structures to improve OOD performance.
papers.key_findings:
Even biased models that exploit spurious correlations contain subnetworks that are less susceptible to these shortcuts.
The functional lottery ticket hypothesis: a full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance when trained in isolation.
Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) effectively learns subnetworks that improve OOD generalization and can be combined with other OOD methods.
Sparsity constraints alone are insufficient for OOD generalization; the structure of the subnetwork is key.
MRM and its variants consistently improve OOD performance across multiple biased datasets.
papers.limitation:
The work has not considered data settings where group attribution information is available (e.g., as in Sagawa et al., 2019).
The experiments use a label noise-free setting, which may not reflect scenarios where spurious features have higher correlation than invariant features.
future_direction: Explore combinations of MRM with different loss designs for subnetwork and model learning.
Extend the approach to data settings with group attribution available.
Investigate the relationship between the structure of digit modules and subsets found by methods like 'and mask' under more domains.
papers.abstract: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? Peters et al. (2016) provides a positive answer for linear cases. In this paper, we use a functional modular probing method to analyze deep model structures under OOD setting. We demonstrate that even in biased models (which focus on spurious correlation) there still exist unbiased functional subnetworks. Furthermore, we articulate and demonstrate the functional lottery ticket hypothesis: full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance. We then propose Modular Risk Minimization to solve the subnetwork selection problem. Our algorithm learns the subnetwork structure from a given dataset, and can be combined with any other OOD regularization methods. Experiments on various OOD generalization tasks corroborate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting.
